Hotel Booking Cancellations — End-to-End Classification Project¶

Goal: predict whether a hotel booking will be canceled (is_canceled = 1) before the guest arrives.

We'll go through six phases:

  1. Data Understanding and Inspection
  2. Data Cleaning (the biggest part)
  3. Data Preprocessing
  4. Data Visualization with Matplotlib
  5. Machine Learning — Logistic Regression, KNN, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Naive Bayes
  6. Model Evaluation

Phase 2: Data Cleaning — Our Biggest Focus¶

Real-world data is messy, and this dataset is no exception. We'll work through it one issue at a time: missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent categories, outliers, wrong data types, and — very important — data leakage.

In [8]:
# Work on a copy so we can always compare back to the raw data if needed.
data = df.copy()
print("Starting shape:", data.shape)

Starting shape: (119390, 32)

# company is ~94% missing. There's really not enough there to learn from,
# so we drop it. (Missing here just means "not a company booking".)
data = data.drop(columns=["company"])

# agent is ~14% missing. Missing means the booking didn't go through a travel agent,
# which is actually useful information! So instead of dropping, we fill with 0 = "no agent".
data["agent"] = data["agent"].fillna(0).astype(int)

# country: only ~0.4% missing. We'll label them "Unknown" rather than throwing rows away.
data["country"] = data["country"].fillna("Unknown")

# children: just 4 missing. Most bookings have no children, so 0 is a safe guess.
data["children"] = data["children"].fillna(0)

print("Missing values left:", data.isna().sum().sum())

Missing values left: 0

# There are a LOT of exact duplicate rows. Some may be genuinely identical group bookings,
# but since there's no booking ID we can't tell them apart, and leaving them in would
# let the same row land in both train and test — which inflates our scores.
# So we drop them.
dup_count = data.duplicated().sum()
print(f"Duplicate rows: {dup_count:,} ({dup_count / len(data):.1%})")

data = data.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

2.4 Impossible / nonsense values¶

In [13]:
# A booking with zero guests (no adults, no children, no babies) doesn't make sense.
no_guests = (data["adults"] + data["children"] + data["babies"]) == 0
print("Bookings with no guests at all:", no_guests.sum())
data = data[~no_guests]

# A stay of 0 nights (no weekend nights AND no week nights) is also odd.
# These are often day-use or data-entry errors, so we remove them too.
zero_nights = (data["stays_in_weekend_nights"] + data["stays_in_week_nights"]) == 0
print("Bookings with 0 nights:", zero_nights.sum())
data = data[~zero_nights]

# A negative daily rate can't happen.
print("Bookings with negative adr:", (data["adr"] < 0).sum())
data = data[data["adr"] >= 0]

print("Shape now:", data.shape)

2.7 Data leakage — the sneaky one¶

Some columns are only known after we already know whether the booking was canceled. If we leave them in, the model will look amazing in testing and be useless in real life.

  • reservation_status is literally "Canceled" / "Check-Out" / "No-Show" — it's the answer itself.
  • reservation_status_date is the date the status was last updated — again, after the fact.
  • assigned_room_type is decided at check-in. Canceled bookings often never get a room assigned (or keep the reserved one), so it quietly leaks the answer.
In [19]:

Phase 3: Data Preprocessing — Advanced Practice¶

Now we turn clean data into something models can learn from: engineer new features, handle skew, tame high-cardinality columns, encode categories, and scale numbers — all without leaking test-set information into training.

3.1 Feature engineering¶

In [21]:
# Total nights and total guests are more intuitive than the split columns.
data["total_nights"] = data["stays_in_weekend_nights"] + data["stays_in_week_nights"]
data["total_guests"] = data["adults"] + data["children"] + data["babies"]

# Families might behave differently from couples or business travelers.
data["has_kids"] = ((data["children"] + data["babies"]) > 0).astype(int)

# Did the guest book through a travel agent at all?
data["has_agent"] = (data["agent"] != 0).astype(int)

# How "trustworthy" is this guest's history? Share of past bookings they canceled.
past_total = data["previous_cancellations"] + data["previous_bookings_not_canceled"]
data["past_cancel_ratio"] = np.where(past_total > 0, data["previous_cancellations"] / past_total, 0)

# Months as names aren't useful to a model; turn them into numbers 1-12.
month_map = {m: i for i, m in enumerate(["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July",
                                         "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"], start=1)}
data["arrival_month"] = data["arrival_date_month"].map(month_map)

# Build an actual arrival date so we can get the day of the week and a weekend flag.
arrival = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=data["arrival_date_year"], month=data["arrival_month"],
                              day=data["arrival_date_day_of_month"]))
data["arrival_weekday"] = arrival.dt.dayofweek  # Monday = 0
data["arrival_on_weekend"] = (data["arrival_weekday"] >= 5).astype(int)

# Seasonality is circular (December sits right next to January), so we encode month
# with sine/cosine. That way the model sees month 12 and month 1 as neighbors.
data["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * data["arrival_month"] / 12)
data["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * data["arrival_month"] / 12)

# Price per person per night is often more meaningful than the raw rate.
data["adr_per_person"] = data["adr"] / data["total_guests"]

# Did the guest ask for any special requests or parking? People who plan details tend to show up.
data["any_special_request"] = (data["total_of_special_requests"] > 0).astype(int)

data[["total_nights", "total_guests", "has_kids", "has_agent", "past_cancel_ratio",
      "arrival_month", "arrival_weekday", "adr_per_person"]].head()

3.2 Taming high-cardinality columns¶

In [22]:
# country has ~170 values and agent has ~300. One-hot encoding all of them would create
# hundreds of mostly-empty columns. Instead we keep the most common ones and group the rest as "Other".
top_countries = data["country"].value_counts().head(15).index
data["country_grouped"] = np.where(data["country"].isin(top_countries), data["country"], "Other")

top_agents = data["agent"].value_counts().head(15).index
data["agent_grouped"] = np.where(data["agent"].isin(top_agents), data["agent"].astype(str), "Other")

# Portugal is the home country of both hotels — domestic guests are a big, distinct group.
data["is_domestic"] = (data["country"] == "PRT").astype(int)

print(data["country_grouped"].value_counts().head(8))

3.3 Choosing features and splitting the data¶

In [23]:
# Drop the raw columns we've replaced with better versions, plus arrival_date_year
# (a model trained on 2015-2017 can't really use "year" to predict the future).
drop_cols = ["is_canceled", "arrival_date_month", "arrival_date_year", "country", "agent",
             "arrival_date_week_number", "arrival_date_day_of_month"]

X = data.drop(columns=drop_cols)
y = data["is_canceled"]

categorical_features = ["hotel", "meal", "market_segment", "distribution_channel", "reserved_room_type",
                        "deposit_type", "customer_type", "country_grouped", "agent_grouped"]
numeric_features = [c for c in X.columns if c not in categorical_features]

print(f"{len(numeric_features)} numeric features, {len(categorical_features)} categorical features")

27 numeric features, 9 categorical features
In [24]:
# Split BEFORE scaling/encoding, so nothing about the test set leaks into training.
# stratify=y keeps the same cancel rate (~27%) in both train and test.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

print("Train:", X_train.shape, " Test:", X_test.shape)
print("Cancel rate — train:", round(y_train.mean(), 3), " test:", round(y_test.mean(), 3))

3.4 Skewness and outlier capping¶

In [25]:
# Several numeric columns are heavily right-skewed (a few huge values, most small).
skew = X_train[numeric_features].skew().sort_values(ascending=False)
skew.head(10)

In [26]:
# Cap extreme values at the 1st and 99th percentile. Importantly, we learn those limits
# from the TRAINING data only and then apply the same limits to the test data.
cap_cols = ["lead_time", "adr", "adr_per_person", "days_in_waiting_list",
            "total_nights", "stays_in_week_nights", "stays_in_weekend_nights", "booking_changes"]

lower = X_train[cap_cols].quantile(0.01)
upper = X_train[cap_cols].quantile(0.99)

X_train = X_train.copy(); X_test = X_test.copy()
X_train[cap_cols] = X_train[cap_cols].clip(lower, upper, axis=1)
X_test[cap_cols] = X_test[cap_cols].clip(lower, upper, axis=1)

# log1p squashes the long right tail of lead_time and waiting time
# (log1p instead of log because these columns contain zeros).
for col in ["lead_time", "days_in_waiting_list"]:
    X_train[col] = np.log1p(X_train[col])
    X_test[col] = np.log1p(X_test[col])

print("Skew after capping + log:")
print(X_train[cap_cols].skew().round(2))

3.5 Encoding and scaling with a ColumnTransformer¶

In [27]:
# One-hot encode categories, standardize numbers. Wrapping this in a ColumnTransformer means
# the exact same steps get applied to train and test, and it's fit on train only.
# handle_unknown="ignore" protects us if a category shows up in test that train never saw.
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), categorical_features),
])

X_train_prep = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_prep = preprocessor.transform(X_test)
feature_names = preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()

print("Final training matrix:", X_train_prep.shape)
print("Final test matrix:    ", X_test_prep.shape)

Final training matrix: (69297, 92)
Final test matrix:     (17325, 92)

Phase 5: Machine Learning Algorithms¶

Seven classifiers, all trained on the same preprocessed data so the comparison is fair. We keep settings sensible rather than heavily tuned — the goal is to see how each family of model behaves.

In [37]:
# The count of negatives / positives — XGBoost can use this to pay a bit more attention to cancellations.
neg_pos_ratio = (y_train == 0).sum() / (y_train == 1).sum()

models = {
    # A great baseline: simple, fast, and the coefficients are easy to interpret.
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),

    # Looks at the 15 most similar bookings and takes a vote. Needs scaled features (we have them).
    # distance weighting = closer neighbors count more.
    "KNN": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15, weights="distance", n_jobs=-1),

    # A single tree. We cap the depth, otherwise it memorizes the training data.
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=12, min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),

    # Lots of trees on random slices of the data, then averaged. Usually very strong out of the box.
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=2, n_jobs=-1,
                                            random_state=RANDOM_STATE),

    # Trees built one after another, each fixing the mistakes of the previous ones.
    "Gradient Boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.1,
                                                    random_state=RANDOM_STATE),

    # A faster, regularized flavor of gradient boosting.
    "XGBoost": XGBClassifier(n_estimators=400, max_depth=7, learning_rate=0.08, subsample=0.9,
                             colsample_bytree=0.8, eval_metric="logloss", n_jobs=-1,
                             random_state=RANDOM_STATE),

    # Assumes features are independent and normally distributed — a strong (wrong) assumption here,
    # so we expect it to struggle, but it's a useful lower-bound reference and it's super fast.
    "Naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
}
In [38]:
# Train each model, predict on the test set, and record the scores.
results = []
trained = {}
probas = {}

for name, model in models.items():
    start = time.time()
    model.fit(X_train_prep, y_train)
    train_time = time.time() - start

    y_pred = model.predict(X_test_prep)
    y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test_prep)[:, 1]

    trained[name] = model
    probas[name] = y_proba
    results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Train accuracy": accuracy_score(y_train, model.predict(X_train_prep)),
        "Test accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "F1": f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, y_proba),
        "Train time (s)": train_time,
    })
    print(f"{name:<20} done in {train_time:5.1f}s  |  test accuracy = {results[-1]['Test accuracy']:.3f}")

Phase 6: Model Evaluation¶

Accuracy alone can be misleading when classes aren't balanced. So we look at:

  • Precision — of the bookings we flagged as "will cancel", how many actually did?
  • Recall — of all the bookings that canceled, how many did we catch?
  • F1 — a balance of the two.
  • ROC-AUC — how well the model ranks risky bookings above safe ones, across all thresholds.

# One test split could be lucky or unlucky. 5-fold cross-validation on the training data gives
# a more trustworthy estimate. We run it for the three strongest models (KNN and boosting with
# sklearn are slow, so we keep this focused).
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
cv_rows = []
for name in results_df.index[:3]:
    scores = cross_val_score(models[name], X_train_prep, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
    cv_rows.append({"Model": name, "CV F1 mean": scores.mean(), "CV F1 std": scores.std()})
    print(f"{name:<20} F1 = {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}")

# Bonus: the default threshold is 0.5, but a hotel might care more about catching cancellations
# (recall) than about false alarms. Here's how precision and recall trade off as we move the threshold.
thresholds = np.arange(0.2, 0.81, 0.05)
best_proba = probas[best_name]
prec = [precision_score(y_test, best_proba >= t) for t in thresholds]
rec = [recall_score(y_test, best_proba >= t) for t in thresholds]
f1s = [f1_score(y_test, best_proba >= t) for t in thresholds]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(thresholds, prec, marker="o", label="Precision", color="#2a6fdb")
ax.plot(thresholds, rec, marker="o", label="Recall", color="#e8743b")
ax.plot(thresholds, f1s, marker="o", label="F1", color="#3a9d5d")
ax.set_xlabel("Decision threshold")
ax.set_ylabel("Score")
ax.set_title(f"Threshold trade-off — {best_name}")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

best_t = thresholds[int(np.argmax(f1s))]
print(f"Best F1 threshold ≈ {best_t:.2f} (F1 = {max(f1s):.3f} vs {f1s[6]:.3f} at 0.50)")
